summary:
Luxembourg recognises gender identity in law through a declaration-based procedure. A person changes gender status and first name(s) in the civil register by application to the Ministry of Justice; no surgery, sterilisation, divorce or other medical treatment is required. The procedure is administered through the official government portal Guichet.lu. Recognition is binary: no nonbinary gender marker is available.

Discrimination law treats "change of sex" as a form of sex discrimination, prohibiting direct and indirect discrimination in employment, education, social security, healthcare and the provision of goods and services. Sexual orientation is separately protected under the Law of 28 November 2006 on equal treatment, covering the same fields. Gender expression and sex characteristics are not protected grounds.

Hate-crime legislation recognises "change of sex" as an aggravating factor, as it does sexual orientation.

Marriage and full adoption rights for same-sex couples took effect on 1 January 2015, after a vote of 56 to 4 in June 2014; registered partnerships carrying many of the benefits of marriage have existed since 1 November 2004. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can marry and adopt in Luxembourg on the same terms as other couples.

The LGBT Action Plan 2018-2023 committed the government to combating violence, harassment and discrimination and to equal treatment in healthcare and employment. In July 2025 the government published a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ Action Plan; organisations criticised it for omitting depathologisation and other key elements. No measures address conversion practices or intersex interventions.

An equality body, CET, handles equal-treatment complaints, and Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale provides services to the LGBTIQ+ community.
tangentialFactors:
The self-determination route replaced a judicial procedure that had been long and costly. Justice Minister Félix Braz presented the bill in May 2017, allowing trans and intersex people to change civil-status gender by declaration; associations welcomed it at the time. The Council of Government approved it on 12 May 2017 and it was submitted to Parliament on 31 May. The Chamber of Deputies approved it by 57 votes to 3 on 25 July 2018, the Council of State consented on 27 July 2018 to dispense with a second vote, the Grand Duke promulgated it on 10 August 2018, it was published in the official journal on 12 September 2018 and it took effect on 16 September 2018.

Before that reform, Luxembourg required surgery, sterilisation and divorce before a change of gender on identification documents.

In June 2019 Le Quotidien reported that the law then lacked LGBTphobic aggravating circumstances, that victims under-reported offences, and that the justice minister had signalled the law would evolve after an intervention by ECRI in 2017. Current legislation recognises "change of sex" as an aggravating factor.
localsOnly:
Minors may apply for a change of gender status with the consent of their legal guardians, including children under the age of five.

Prison authorities place detainees who disclose or openly show an LGBT or trans identity so that they are sheltered from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners. Trans detainees' situations are handled case by case, with the administration gathering all available information on the prisoner; such cases are described as exceptional. Requests by LGBT detainees to be placed in an ordinary section are generally granted, and the minister warned against solutions that would stigmatise or isolate these detainees.

A 1989 grand-ducal regulation requires staff to address detainees by surname, and penitentiary staff honour a detainee's chosen "Monsieur" or "Madame" form of address. The Justice Ministry keeps no statistics on LGBT prisoners, on the basis that disclosure cannot be compelled without unlawful interference with privacy. The planned Uerschterhaff prison at Sanem was designed with multiple sections allowing detainees to be separated by sex, personality, grounds of detention and sexual orientation. Placement follows disclosed identity and need on a case-by-case basis; no codified birth-sex rule and no special custody unit or solitary or administrative segregation for trans prisoners is documented.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the declaration procedure is open to non-residents, and what documentation a foreign national must produce, is not established by the sources reviewed.

Enforcement data on prosecutions or sentences involving "change of sex" as an aggravating factor is not available in the sources reviewed.

The specific commitments of the July 2025 LGBTIQ+ Action Plan and its implementation status are not detailed in the sources reviewed.
